To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

monolingual Spanish speakers use suprasegmental prosodic cues (stress) to anticipate word suffix (morphology) during lexical access, and that late learners can qualitatively, though not quantitatively (i.e. as well as monolinguals), use prosodic cues to anticipate word suffix during lexical access.

monolinguals use prosodic information in anticipation of word suffixes, but that beginning learners do not use this information to predict word morphology, and that advanced learners use prosodic information, but only in certain conditions, and only after extensive practice with the language.
the monolinguinguals used prosody to anticipate word endings in both visual-world eye-tracking (VWE) and gating (G) tasks, regardless of word stress or word structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of morphological processing in L1 and L2, and how suprasegmental cues can facilitate the development of anticipatory processing in L2.
the role that prosody plays during morphological processing in monolinguals as compared to L1/L2 bilinguals.
the development of anticipatory lexical processing in L2 Spanish, and its relationship with proficiency and WM.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the monolingually acquired prosodic information is used for morphological anticipation in the native language, and that the prosodic information is acquired in the non-native language, although it does not seem to be used for morphological anticipatory processing in the L2.
L2 learners can gain the ability to predict morphological information from prosodic information, but only after extensive exposure and practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prosodic and morphological processing is tightly intertwined, and that L2 proficiency, but not WM, can facilitate morphological anticipation during lexical access.
the ability to use prosodic cues to facilitate morphological anticipation in L1 is not necessarily transferred to L2.
the monolinguinguals and the advanced learners used suprasegmental cues to anticipate morphological suffixes in both tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prosodic information can be used to facilitate morphological processing in L2 learners, even when the learners are at an intermediate level of proficiency.
L2 learners can acquire prosodic cues for morphological anticipation, but they need to be highly proficient in order to achieve this.
L2 proficiency is a key factor in the acquisition of prosodically-based morphological processing, and that this process is not necessarily related to WM capacity.
